chapter.name: Living Creatures: Exploring their Characteristics
chapter.blurb: A shift from comparing everyday living and non-living things (a pencil, a book, a pigeon, a car, a plant) to naming the eight characteristics shared by all living beings -- movement, need for food, growth, respiration, excretion, response to stimuli, reproduction and eventual death -- through hands-on activities: testing which conditions let a bean seed germinate, tracking how a seedling's root and shoot always grow down and up regardless of how the seed is oriented, following a bean plant's life cycle from seed to pod and back to seed, and comparing the four-stage life cycles of a mosquito (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and a frog (egg, tadpole, froglet, adult).

scope_in.item: Identify everyday things (a pencil, a book, a pigeon, a car, a plant) as living or non-living and give a reason
State the characteristics common to living beings: they move, need food, grow, respire, excrete, respond to stimuli, reproduce, and eventually die; absence of these indicates a non-living thing
Recognise movement in plants that does not involve changing location -- the opening of flowers, the leaf-trapping action of an insectivorous plant like Drosera, and climbers winding around a support
Explain growth as a shared characteristic of living beings, using the example of outgrowing childhood clothes
Describe breathing/respiration in humans (inhaling and exhaling air) and in plants (air moving in and out through stomata on the leaf surface)
Describe excretion in humans (sweat, urine) and in plants (excess water and minerals removed as small droplets, e.g. on grass and rose leaves)

Describe response to stimuli using examples: touch-me-not (chhui-mui/mimosa/lajjalu) folding its leaves when touched, amla leaves folding after sunset, and a person withdrawing from a thorn or a hot cup
State reproduction as producing new ones of one's own kind, necessary for the continuity of life
State the chapter's description of death: when a living being cannot show the characteristics of life even though food, air and water are available
Identify the conditions essential for seed germination -- water (softens the seed coat and lets the embryo develop) and air (from the spaces between soil particles, which also let roots grow easily)
State that presence or absence of light generally does not affect whether a seed germinates, but sunlight is needed for the seedling's growth after germination
Describe Activity 10.3's set-up and results: the direction of growth of the root and shoot of a seedling kept upright, kept inverted, and lit from only one direction
State the conclusion that shoots grow upward and bend towards light, while roots always grow downward, whichever way the plant is positioned
Recall Jagadish Chandra Bose and the crescograph, a machine he built to record how plants respond to stimuli such as light, heat, electricity and gravity, and to measure their growth

Describe the life cycle of a bean plant: seed, germination, appearance of leaves, appearance of flowers, appearance of fruit (a pod containing seeds), and death, with the seeds starting a new generation
Describe the four stages in the life cycle of a mosquito -- egg, larva, pupa, adult -- and that larvae and pupae live in water but come to the surface for air
Explain how stagnant water lets mosquitoes breed and how a layer of kerosene oil on water kills larvae and pupae by cutting off their air supply

Describe the four main stages in the life cycle of a frog -- egg/spawn, tadpole (an early stage with a tail and no legs, then a later stage with hind legs), froglet, adult -- and the shift in habitat towards land

State the chapter's summary facts: the eight characteristics of living beings, germination's dependence on water and air (not light), root-down/shoot-up growth, and the specific life-cycle stages of a mosquito and a frog

concepts.name: Characteristics that set living beings apart from non-living things
concepts.description: Comparing living beings and non-living things through everyday examples to identify the characteristics shared by living things.
concepts.idea: Living beings show a set of characteristics -- movement, need for food, growth, respiration, excretion, response to stimuli and reproduction -- and eventually die; a thing lacking these is non-living.
concepts.rule: All living beings move (even plants show movement, such as opening flowers, folding leaves, or an insectivorous plant like Drosera trapping insects, without changing location), need food (nutrition) for growth, grow in size, respire (breathe air in and out; plants use stomata on their leaves), excrete waste (humans through sweat and urine; plants excrete excess water and minerals as droplets, e.g. on grass or rose leaves), respond to stimuli (e.g. a touch-me-not plant folding its leaves when touched, or amla leaves folding after sunset), and reproduce to produce new ones of their own kind, maintaining continuity of life. When a living being can no longer show these characteristics even though food, air and water are available, it is said to be dead.
concepts.example: A car can move but cannot grow, respire, excrete, respond to stimuli or reproduce, so it is non-living; a touch-me-not plant folds its leaves when touched, showing response to a stimulus even though it cannot walk.

concepts.name: Essential conditions for seed germination
concepts.description: Using Activity 10.2's pot experiment to identify the conditions a seed needs to germinate.
concepts.idea: A seed needs the right conditions -- water and air, but generally not light -- to germinate, that is, to turn into a sprout.
concepts.rule: Seeds need water, which softens the seed coat and lets the tiny embryo inside develop into a plant. Seeds also need air, which they get from the spaces between soil particles; these same spaces also let roots grow easily. For most seeds, including bean seeds, the presence or absence of light does not affect germination itself, though after germination, sunlight is needed for the seedling to grow further. In Activity 10.2, four pots of bean seeds were kept under different combinations of water, sunlight and darkness to test which conditions matter.
concepts.example: A pot with no water, even in bright sunlight, does not germinate because seeds need water to soften the seed coat; a pot with moist soil kept in the dark can still germinate because light is not essential for germination.

concepts.name: Growth and movement in plants
concepts.description: Using Activity 10.3 to see how the root and shoot of a plant grow in fixed directions, and how the shoot bends towards light.
concepts.idea: Roots and shoots of a germinating plant grow in fixed directions regardless of how the seedling is oriented, and shoots bend towards light.
concepts.rule: When a plant is kept upright, the root grows downwards and the shoot grows upwards. When the plant is kept inverted, the root still bends and grows downwards, and the shoot still bends and grows upwards. When a plant receives sunlight from only one direction, the shoot grows and bends towards that light while the root continues to grow downwards. So shoots grow upward and move towards sunlight, while roots always grow downward. Jagadish Chandra Bose built a machine called a crescograph to record how plants respond to stimuli like light, heat, electricity and gravity, and to measure how fast plants grow.
concepts.example: A seedling placed upside down in a beaker still grows its root downward and its shoot upward, bending as needed to do so.

concepts.name: Life cycle of a plant
concepts.description: Tracking a bean plant from seed to fruit and back to a new generation of seeds, as a life cycle.
concepts.idea: A plant's life passes through fixed stages from seed to a new generation of seeds.
concepts.rule: A bean seed germinates into a young plant, which grows leaves, then matures to produce flowers, and then fruit (a pod containing seeds). The seeds inside the fruit can be sown to grow a new generation of bean plants, so the cycle continues. This entire process, from a seed to a plant, and then to the next generation of seeds, is called the life cycle of a plant. When a plant stops growing and all its life activities end, even though all necessary conditions are available, it is considered dead.
concepts.example: A bean seed grows into a plant with leaves, flowers and pods; the seeds from the pod can be sown to start the cycle again in a new generation of plants.

concepts.name: Life cycle of a mosquito
concepts.description: The four stages of a mosquito's life cycle, its dependence on stagnant water, and how this is used to control breeding.
concepts.idea: A mosquito passes through four distinct stages of a life cycle, mostly in water.
concepts.rule: Mosquitoes pass through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. The adult female mosquito lays eggs directly on or near water. Eggs develop into larvae, larvae grow into pupae, and pupae transform into adult mosquitoes, which emerge, rest briefly on the water surface, then fly away and survive about 10 to 15 days. Larvae and pupae live in water but need air to respire, so they repeatedly come to the water surface for air. A thin layer of kerosene oil poured on stagnant water separates the water from air, so larvae and pupae cannot inhale air and die -- this is used to control mosquito breeding, along with avoiding stagnant water.
concepts.example: Kerosene poured on a puddle's surface stops mosquito larvae and pupae from breathing air, killing them and breaking the life cycle.

concepts.name: Life cycle of a frog
concepts.description: The four main stages of a frog's life cycle, and how its habitat shifts from water towards land.
concepts.idea: A frog also passes through four main stages in its life cycle, moving from water to land.
concepts.rule: A frog's eggs are laid in a jelly-like cluster called spawn, near or in a pond. The four main stages are the egg (which develops through an embryo stage), the tadpole stage (an early stage with a tail and no legs, using the tail to swim, then a later stage with hind legs, still living in water), the froglet stage (looking like a small frog, still living mostly in water but starting to spend time on land, with the tail shrinking and the legs growing stronger), and the adult frog stage (fully developed, having lost the tail completely, able to jump, and living both in water and on land). Such changes in body shape, structure and habitat during a life cycle are important for animals to survive and continue their kind.
concepts.example: A tadpole uses its tail to swim in water; as it becomes a froglet and then an adult frog, it loses its tail and gains strong legs for jumping on land.
